The Legislative Branch. Formally known as Congress, the federal authority vested with the power to make laws in the United States government. Established by Article I of the Constitution, Congress comprises the House of Representatives and the Senate and serves as the primary vehicle through which the American people, through their elected representatives, exercise sovereign power.

Congress consists of two chambers: the House of Representatives with four hundred thirty-five voting members apportioned by population, and the Senate with one hundred members, two from each state. This bicameral structure was a compromise between small and large states at the Constitutional Convention.

The legislative branch holds the power of the purse—authority to levy taxes, appropriate funds, and authorize government spending. This financial control is the legislature's most potent check on executive power. Congress possesses exclusive power to enact laws affecting interstate commerce, regulate currency, establish federal courts, declare war, raise armies, and regulate naturalization. These powers define the federal government's scope.

The House of Representatives initiates revenue bills, reflecting the Framers' belief that this chamber, with its shorter terms and larger, more numerous membership, best represents popular will on fiscal matters. House members serve two-year terms and stand for election frequently, making them responsive to current public opinion. Senators serve six-year staggered terms, insulating the Senate from sudden electoral swings.

The legislative process requires bills to pass both chambers and be signed by the President. Congress may override a presidential veto with a two-thirds supermajority in both chambers, demonstrating legislative independence. The legislature cannot unilaterally amend the Constitution; such changes require proposal by two-thirds of both chambers or by a constitutional convention, then ratification by three-fourths of state legislatures, a deliberately difficult threshold.

Congress operates through a committee system where detailed legislative work occurs, allowing specialization and compromise to happen before the full chambers vote on negotiated final versions.
